stories.headline: Mexico City Grand Prix 2026: Race start time, how to watch, full schedule, predictions
stories.summary: Formula 1 heads to Mexico on a weekend where Kimi Antonelli could win the drivers' championship for the first time.
stories.body:
Formula 1 heads to Mexico on a weekend where Kimi Antonelli could win the drivers' championship for the first time.

The Mercedes driver extended his lead in the title to 123 points from George Russell after winning the United States Grand Prix. He will simply need to finish ninth or higher in Mexico City to seal the title.

Ferrari's Charles Leclerc was looking strong in the upgraded Ferrari to finish second in Austin, with Max Verstappen on the final step of the podium.

So you don't miss a thing, here's everything you need to know for the 19th round.

- F1 readies Antonelli's title champagne in Austin: 'The race of a champion who isn't champion yet'

- How Kimi Antonelli can win F1 title at Mexico GP -- with or without Qatar, Abu Dhabi races

- George Russell: Finishing second in F1 title race 'doesn't mean anything'

Mexico City Grand Prix schedule
All times in GMT

Friday, October 30

Practice One: 6.30 p.m. - 7.30 p.m.

Practice Two: 10 p.m. - 11 p.m.

Saturday, October 31

Final Practice: 5.30 p.m. - 6.30 p.m.

Qualifying: 9 p.m. - 10 p.m.

Sunday, November 1

Mexico Grand Prix: 8 p.m.

How to watch

Every practice and qualifying session as well as the race itself will be available to watch on Sky Sports F1. The sessions are also on Sky Sports Main Event.

For non-subscribers, highlights of the Mexico City Grand Prix will be on free-to-air television on Channel 4.

In the U.S., subscribers can watch every session on Apple TV, via a new F1 channel on the platform.

Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez
Mexico City is one of the most vibrant atmospheres on the calendar and fans congregate in the thousands to cheer on home hero Sergio Pérez.

It's a true anomaly on the calendar due to the high altitude of of 7,300 feet (2,200 metres) and therefore presents a unique challenge for the teams and drivers. Teams can run Monaco-level downforce packages while still reaching Monza-esque top speeds.

One of the iconic parts of the track -- the Foro Sol stadium section -- includes two tight corners in a former baseball stadium.

Mexico City Grand Prix

Circuit: Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez; Mexico City, Mexico

Previous winners in Mexico

2015: Nico Rosberg (Mercedes)

2016: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2017: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2018: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2019: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2021: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2022: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2023: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2024: Carlos Sainz (Ferrari)

2025: Lando Norris (McLaren)

Other key stats

First F1 race: 1963

Laps: 71 laps of 4.3km

Lap record: 1:17.774, Valtteri Bottas (2021)

Most wins: Verstappen with five (2017-2018, 2021-2023). Other winners from the current grid are Hamilton (2016, 2019), Sainz (2024) and Norris (2025).

Most poles: Jim Clark with four (1963-1965, 1967). Other pole sitters from the current grid are Hamilton (2016), Leclerc (2019, 2023), Verstappen (2022), Sainz (2024) and Norris (2025).

Weather forecast

The weather for the Mexico City Grand Prix is set to reach temperatures of 27°C for qualifying and Sunday's race, with no rain due.

What happened last time out?
Norris pulled out a thrilling lap to take pole position in Mexico, his first pole since the Belgian Grand Prix in July. The Brit said on the team radio afterwards "What a lap. What a lap. Even I don't know how I did that."

It was a dominant race weekend from the McLaren driver after he became the new leader in the title race ahead of his teammate Oscar Piastri for the first time since April.

He had a one point advantage over Piastri with just four races to go.

Who will win this year?

Antonelli put his Mercedes on a surprise pole in Austin and converted it into another victory as he inches closer to taking the title crown with five races remaining.

The youngster will need just two points this weekend, or for Russell and Hamilton to not win the race, to get the job done in Mexico.

Red Bull are a looming threat each weekend after bringing major upgrades and Verstappen will be one to watch out for. He's also got five race victories under his belt around Mexico City.

All eyes will be on Antonelli. He will be hoping to wrap up the title and is looking like he's in a position where nobody will be able to stop him.

stories.headline: How Milwaukee Brewers became 2026 World Series champions
stories.summary: The 2026 Brewers fulfilled their mission -- and will never be forgotten.
stories.body:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. -- Christian Yelich knew the question was coming. Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy occasionally gathers a group of player leaders for a get-together to ensure everyone, in his parlance, "is on the bus" -- together, committed, unified -- and he began the July 29 meeting with the same question he does every time: "What ya got?"

Yelich had settled on his answer and understood its significance. He is no braggart, preferring to endear through humility, a rare characteristic for a former MVP. This was not going to be humble. The Brewers -- everything they stood for, everything they were, everything they aspired to be -- had compelled him to speak his truth, and that truth, coming from the mouth of the man who two months later would be named the team's captain, became their ethos when Yelich answered first.

"We're going to win the World Series," he said.

It's easy for a player to suggest that, easier to think it. Not Christian Yelich, who at 34 is too wise, too wizened, to speak in declarative statements. What-ya-got meetings are not typically the place for such decrees, either, but Murphy encouraged the men in the room -- hitters and pitchers, American and Latin American, young and old -- to speak their truths. Yelich believed to his core that these Brewers were going to purge a half-century of history with one magnificent run.

Because the bus was humming. On that date, the Brewers carried the second-best record in Major League Baseball, a game back of the defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers, who the previous season had shamed Milwaukee during a four-game sweep in the National League Championship Series. Yelich was convinced these Brewers were different. They had made the postseason seven of the previous eight years, and never had he suggested they would emerge from October with baseball's ultimate prize. Now, he meant what he said, and he wanted to make sure the others in the room were just as convicted as him. So he followed with a question of his own: "Do you guys all want to agree to that?"

Around the room they went. Catcher William Contreras, the Brewers' id, said yes. So did his emotional counterbalance, the ever-steady Brice Turang. Brandon Woodruff, the longest-tenured Brewer, the person who more than anyone recognized what fulfilling this pledge would mean to the city of Milwaukee and state of Wisconsin and universe of baseball, affirmed it. Aaron Ashby, Jake Bauers, Sal Frelick, Trevor Megill: yes, yes, yes, yes.

"Murph," Yelich said, "are you on board, too? We're gonna win the World Series?"

More than four decades in baseball had taught the 67-year-old Murphy certain things, such as: Do not tempt the baseball gods with hubristic edicts. In his head, Murphy wasn't yet on board. He had seen too much baseball to think with such certitude. But as much as Murphy values brutal honesty, he saw something happening in that room. All the faith -- in themselves, in this thing they'd spent the past decade building. "It's just about the group," Murphy said, "because if the group is right, the rest of them will be right." Murphy sheathed his sharp tongue, which had at one point or another expertly cut through every person in the room, and boarded Yelich's bus with a yes.

"You speak it into existence, and you establish the fact that this is what we're going to do," Yelich said. "We've decided as a group we're going to do this, and now everything from this point forward is to accomplish that goal, whether that's holding each other accountable, whether that's making sure we get to early work, whether that's making sure we're all at team stretch. All the little details are because we're going to win the World Series. And it makes it easy to have a standard and go forth with the rest of the year when you refer to it like that."

The Brewers' work ended Wednesday night in front of 40,489 people at Tropicana Field, upward of half riding shotgun on Milwaukee's bus. Wearing every incarnation of Brewers jerseys and hats, Milwaukee fans had taken over the Tampa Bay Rays' stadium to witness something that had taken over half a century. This was a different sort of meeting, one that brought together one endlessly loyal group of believers in the stands with another on the field.

What ya got? Exactly what Christian Yelich presaged nearly three months to the day earlier: a World Series championship.

FOR THE PAST 57 years, the Milwaukee Brewers were baseball peasants. Perpetually overlooked and terminally underfunded, they existed mostly as an afterthought outside of Wisconsin, a state filled with inhabitants whose defining feature is their civic pride. When the Brewers were bad, they were quite bad. When they were good, it came with a caveat: They were still not as good as the game's blue bloods -- the New York Yankees, the aforementioned Dodgers and, too many times for anyone's liking, the loathed Chicago Cubs.

Fans believed anyway because what choice did they have? Give up? Abscond? Hell no. Not Wisconsin. Never Wisconsin. And to be clear, as much as the Brewers are Milwaukee's team by name, they are Wisconsin's by birthright, which is why their 4-1 victory over the Rays in Game 5 sent aftershocks to the state's more than 50,000 square miles. Decades of agony, salved by a month of near perfection.

Of the 122 postseasons played in MLB, few have included such an obvious gap between the winner and the rest. The Brewers trampled the Rays, same as they had filleted the Dodgers, which they did after dispatching the San Diego Padres. They imposed themselves with authority and suffered minimal pushback. Over the month of October, Milwaukee went 11-2, outscored opponents 59-33 and posted an OPS nearly 250 points higher than it allowed. Both of the Brewers' losses came by one run.

Carrying the 19th-highest payroll in the game, living in the 30th-ranked market of the 30 MLB teams, the Brewers came together in piecemeal fashion. Operating on a small budget is strenuous. Thriving in a small market is grueling. Attempting to do both simultaneously is a recipe for sorrow. Between their last run to the World Series in 1982 and the launch of the current era that began with an NLCS trip in 2018, the Brewers vacillated between bad and not quite as bad. Though sporadic success sustained the organization, deep down everyone understood the insufficiency of it all.

So the Brewers did something antithetical to the warm, loving squeeze of the Midwest: They embraced the cold, ruthless efficiency of modern baseball team-building in a small market. The Rays were the model, sustaining success over nearly two decades by developing players and flipping them at the apex of their value or as free agency neared. Milwaukee leaned into the model, trading an All-Star each of the past four seasons. In the meantime, the original architect of the Brewers' resurgence, David Stearns, left to run the New York Mets, and the manager who grew up in Wisconsin, Craig Counsell, decamped for the Cubs.

At the helm for most of the moves was Matt Arnold, the Brewers' president of baseball operations. With a biting sense of humor and deep streak of independence -- he has clung to his Android phone as his underlings, friends and even his teenage daughter ridiculed him as a green texter -- Arnold had parlayed a successful scouting career into a front office role that necessitated excellence in all areas to breed continuous contention.

"He created this team, so I'm just very proud that he selected me to be a part of it," said Jackson Chourio, the 22-year-old whose 11 hits in the World Series were more than one-third of what the entire Rays team logged over the five games. "And it seems kind of like everyone he picks, it works out."

Arnold was in the room the day Yelich declared the Brewers' destiny, and the timing couldn't have been more complicated. Three days later, he received a call he had been expecting: The Detroit Tigers were trading Tarik Skubal, arguably the best pitcher in baseball, and between their major league roster and top-of-the-sport farm system, the Brewers had the talent to land him and pair him with soon-to-be NL Cy Young Award winner Jacob Misiorowski. Such a deal would run counter to Milwaukee's operating philosophy, but then this was Tarik Skubal.

Over the next 24 hours, the Brewers considered whether to meet Detroit's demand of rookie right-hander Logan Henderson as any potential deal's centerpiece. Arnold weighed the benefits and detriments of such a trade and landed in the same place to which Yelich had guided him days earlier.

"I really did believe in the group," Arnold said, "and when you talk about certain names, whoever that is, like big-time guys that might be left-handed and throw hard and have Cy Young Awards, hypothetically, those guys might help. But it's also like: We've got a lot of good dudes in the room already, you know? I really do believe in them.

"And here we are."

WINNING A WORLD Series is not some linear exercise. Not over the course of building a title-contending team, and especially not in a 162-game season in which the best teams still get beaten 40% of the time. In the hours after Yelich pronounced the Brewers future champions, they lost 16-3 to a San Francisco Giants team that finished 65-97, the fourth-worst record in baseball.

Yelich's belief never flagged because he knew who the Brewers were: the product of the Pat Murphy school of baseball. They hustled -- and if they didn't, Murphy benched them. They deified clean, fundamental ball. They led MLB in batting average and walk rate. They chased pitches outside the strike zone less than any other team. They homered enough. And after the shellacking in San Francisco, they went an MLB-best 36-18 over the final third of the season. Murphy paved the road so Yelich could drive the bus. With an MLB-best 103 regular-season wins, Milwaukee secured a first-round bye, only to face the other team that had won two-thirds of its final 54 games, San Diego, in the wild-card round.

Before that series, Yelich was talking with Dan Vogelbach, one of the Brewers' hitting coaches and a nine-year major league veteran. Vogelbach made a prediction: Whoever won that division series was going to win the World Series. With a little fortune -- Ty France's potential home run clanging off a roof cable at Milwaukee's American Family Field in Game 1 remains an all-timer -- and a lot of skill, the Brewers disposed of the Padres in four games. Next up were the two-time defending World Series champion Dodgers.

"We wanted to play them," Yelich said. "We didn't want to win a World Series without going through them. That's not a slight to anybody else, but it's like: These are the champs. They've been the guy that's been standing in the way these last few years. We want to go through them. And we're ready."

That preparedness took time -- and pain. The NLCS last year did a number on the Brewers. They scored four runs in the entire series. They arrived happy to be there and left sad at their showing. The winter bred desire for vengeance. Not to slake any leftover animus, but to prove to themselves that everything they stand for, everything they believe, isn't so fragile that a $500 million-plus team can simply money-slap them.

All of the slapping in this year's NLCS came at the Brewers' hands. They weren't just the better team. The Brewers were the bullies, coming back from deficits in all four games, turning a seeming juggernaut into a puddle of goo. The Dodgers didn't take Milwaukee lightly, either. The Brewers were simply better, reciprocating with a four-game sweep of their own. If Murphy wasn't a believer before, the Dodgers series convinced him.

"When I saw the way we responded to the Dodgers," he said, "I'm like, 'Damn, I wonder who's gonna win the American League, because we're gonna win this.' And then, sure as hell, the first two games, the way they went down, it's amazing."

ON AUG. 1, 2022, the Brewers traded Josh Hader to the San Diego Padres. At the time, they were 57-45 and owners of a three-game lead in the NL Central. Over the next two months, they played sub-.500 ball and finished seven games behind the St. Louis Cardinals. Fans grew furious, incapable of knowing the deal would catalyze their first championship. In the trade, the Brewers received speedy outfielder Esteury Ruiz. Five months later, they shipped him out as part of a three-way deal that netted them a 25-year-old catcher named William Contreras.

Contreras won World Series MVP on Wednesday. Chourio also could have won with little opposition. Same with rookie shortstop Cooper Pratt, who strung together six consecutive hits between Games 4 and 5, or reliever Aaron Ashby, who ended the postseason with 18 scoreless innings. Beyond his eight hits, Contreras struck out just once in 23 plate appearances and turned in an exceptional defensive effort, nailing 10 of 13 ABS challenges -- many of which flipped an at-bat from the Rays' favor to the Brewers' -- and throwing out three attempted base stealers.

"I always tell him, 'Don't do what I've done. I want you to be the best. I want you to be better,'" said Willson Contreras, the All-Star first baseman for the Boston Red Sox and Contreras' older brother. "And now that I'm on this side, I'm learning from him. I'm learning a lot from him, and it makes me proud of the player he has become and the player he's going to be during his whole career.

"He controls his emotions a lot better. That's one thing that I always tell him: Control your emotions because when the tensions are high, it's really easy to lose your focus. It's toughness. Mindset. Focused energy. He knows how to manage his game as well. You can be a catcher and be all over the place like I was. Or to be a catcher like him who's already settled and knows what he's doing and is always looking to learn and willing to listen. And that's what makes baseball players better."

William was the youngest of the three Contreras boys growing up in Puerto Cabello, Venezuela, a coastal city in a baseball-mad country. As the baby, he was "the spoiled one," Willson said, later tagging along to watch him or their eldest brother, Wilmer, play ball. William revered his brothers, and, at 20 years old, he wrote Willson a note of appreciation that included six words he still remembers to this day: "You are my example to follow."

"I still have that letter back home," Willson said, "and that put some kind of pressure on myself to be the best for him."

He couldn't help but think of it during Contreras' sixth-inning at-bat against Garrett Cleavinger in Game 5. The Contreras brothers had played together during Venezuela's World Baseball Classic triumph earlier this year. William had lived through the vise of baseball with profound meaning before. To see him so calmly and casually stroke an RBI double into the left-field corner to extend Milwaukee's lead to three runs, though, left Willson bouncing in the stands -- replete with Contreras' No. 24 Brewers jersey -- as it took the Brewers one step closer to doing something Willson did as a rookie in 2016 with a Cubs team that broke a championship drought nearly twice as long as Milwaukee's.

"They're a great team from top to bottom," Willson said. "They have a great manager, Pat Murphy. He keeps everybody accountable. He knows how to manage a great team like he has. They have a really good depth, and with the depth they have, it was tough to win against them.

"I don't care if I have to put a Brewers jersey on. I respect what this team has done. I respect every player. One thing when we play against each other is being a fan. I'm a fan of them, and they play really good. They deserve to be here."

His brother wasn't the only gem uncovered by Arnold's staff. The Brewers traded for Megill and DL Hall, two of their half-dozen relief pitchers capable of throwing triple-digit fastballs. They got Robert Gasser, author of six scoreless innings in Game 3, in the Hader trade. They nailed their first-round picks with Turang and Frelick and Garrett Mitchell. They raided the Kansas City area for Misiorowski (second round in 2022) and Ashby (fourth round in 2018). They stole Henderson in the fourth and Pratt in the sixth in other drafts. And, at Arnold's behest, they completely revamped their international scouting apparatus, going from a nonfactor to among the best in baseball, with 31 scouts scouring the Dominican Republic and Venezuela for the next generation of Brewers stars.

Chourio, part of Team Venezuela with the Contreras brothers, was the first to hit big. He rocketed through the organization, becoming one of the game's top prospects in 2022. The Brewers so deeply trusted in his future stardom that they guaranteed him $82 million over eight years before his debut. Like Contreras, he thrust himself into the spotlight throughout October, piecing line drives all over the diamond, blazing around the basepaths with purpose -- and good-naturedly chirping his teammates to remind them exactly who he is because it so perfectly dovetails with who the Brewers are.

"Whenever I do something well, I say I'm the best," Chourio said. "I'm the best in the world. There's no one better than me. It's kind of humorous. But also, you know, I think words have power. And I'm just instilling that in myself as well."

THE BUZZ AT American Family Field was as abundant as the Miller Lite empties in the parking lots surrounding the stadium. The first World Series game in Milwaukee in more than four decades served as a reminder for those outside of Wisconsin that great baseball teams need not come from the coasts. Small-market success isn't an oxymoron. Low-payroll excellence isn't an impossibility. With the owners prepared to shut down the sport when the current collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1 because of players' refusal to accept a salary cap the league claims is necessary to support such teams, the upstart World Series would be a timely rejoinder.

Following a 3-2 win in Game 1 and 5-4 win in Game 2 that flipped with five unanswered runs by the Brewers, the series moved to the Trop, where Milwaukee intended to finish its charge. By then, Yelich was convinced his claim wasn't just a mantra or rallying cry. This was cosmic, replete with tobacco totems. Before Game 3, as he walked down the tunnel toward the dugout, Yelich smelled a familiar odor emanating from the batting cage. Rally heaters were aflame.

Though cigarette use has dropped precipitously, every clubhouse in MLB features at least one player who relishes a dart now and again. The Brewers regard them as good-luck charms. Before every game, regardless of where they are, plumes of smoke twist in the air as Milwaukee hitters prepare in the cage for the contest ahead. The rationale is ridiculously perfect and perfectly ridiculous: If they smoke heaters in the cage, they'll smoke heaters in the game. And they did. In the World Series, Milwaukee hit .278 with a .742 OPS against fastballs. The Rays hit .159 and OPS'd .395.

"You walk by the cage and see the cigs lit," Yelich said, "and you're like, the boys are ready to rock."

The full essence of these Brewers revealed itself in Game 3 during an eight-run fifth inning. Seven consecutive two-out hits fueled it and turned a 2-0 contest into a 10-0 woodshedding. They were up three games to none in a best-of-seven series. No team in the World Series ever had erased such a deficit. Only four of the 25 facing such a deficit had won the fourth game. Tampa Bay looked cooked when Pratt homered in the top of the 12th inning the following night, only to storm back with four consecutive hits, including a walk-off Baltimore chop to the right side by Ben Williamson to win Game 4 and keep its season alive. In the clubhouse after the game, Yelich waited until his whole team filed in to address the letdown.

"This wasn't supposed to be easy," he said. "Nothing's guaranteed. It's the World Series. All we can do is focus on tomorrow. Today's over. There's nothing we can do. Just flip the page. We have a great opportunity ahead of us, and it starts now."

Panic isn't in the Brewers' DNA. They are acutely aware of who they are. They don't have a 40-home run bopper. They don't have a particularly deep starting rotation. They make up for it with everything else. And in Game 5, they sent Misiorowski to the mound. Though he didn't generate swing-and-miss commensurate to a regular season in which he held the MLB strikeout crown, he proved difficult for the Rays to square up over the 5⅔ innings he threw before a calf cramp prompted his removal from the game. By that point, the Brewers held a four-run lead, with a pair of RBIs from Pratt, and Murphy gladly handed the game over to his bullpen, which over 65 postseason innings posted a 1.38 ERA.

JoJo Romero closed out the sixth and got an out in the seventh, with Abner Uribe coming on for the final two outs of the frame. Closer Megill pitched the final two innings, allowing a run in the ninth before inducing a weak groundball that Turang threw to Bauers for the final out. The Brewers exulted. Milwaukee heaved. Wisconsin palpitated. The baseball world nodded out of respect for a team worthy of being called champion.

Brewers players wanted to share the spoils with their adoring admirers. Pratt, full of vim and vigor, sprinted out of the clubhouse celebration lugging the commissioner's trophy. "Go! Go! Go!" he yelled, dashing to the tunnel, where he singsonged: "We are the champions, my friend." Down the steps and onto the field, Pratt thrust the piece of metal into the air and was greeted with a hero's welcome.

The thousands of Brewers fans lucky enough to bear witness crammed themselves into seemingly every seat down the third-base line at Tropicana Field for a glimpse at their conquerors. Some wore foam cowboy hats constructed to resemble cheese, and others carried signs ("For my dad!" or "For Ueck," franchise icon Bob Uecker), and all had traveled from somewhere, the Brewers' gravitational pull resonant across generations.

All the while, Murphy was bouncing from admirer to admirer. His presence spawned glee and tears and everything in between. His face, ruddy and weathered, its creases earned, twists into shapes that suggest exactly how he's feeling. He saw Yelich and meandered over.

"Told you we were gonna do it," Murphy said, smiling as he held in one hand a carafe that had "Relentless" printed on the side and in his back pocket the lineup card for the day. Murphy has done just about everything in baseball. He won 1,000 games coaching in college. He managed in the minor leagues. He served as Counsell's bench coach. And now he's a World Series-winning manager, a distinction shared by only three other current managers.

"It all starts with Murph, man," Vogelbach said. "I'll say it again: He's the best leader of people I've ever been around, and it's not even close."

WHAT'S PARTICULARLY TERRIFYING about this Brewers team isn't how handily it dominated the best of what baseball has to offer. It's that there's a real path to this being the beginning of something much longer-lasting than the dopamine bomb of the first World Series championship in a franchise's history. Chourio and Pratt are both 22. Nobody in the Brewers' rotation is eligible to reach free agency for another three years. And whether it's infielder Jesús Made -- the top overall prospect in MLB -- minor league home run king Andrew Fischer or highly regarded infielder Luis Peña, reinforcements for the Brewers are coming, allowing them to cycle out aging and expensive players, if they desire, or amplify what they've already got.

"Keep going and keep winning more championships," Chourio said. "It's an organization that's put in their everything. So it brings a lot of joy to see us be able to bring a championship for them as well."

The Brewers did it their way, and there's a particular satisfaction in that. Batters hit just four home runs in the 2026 World Series, the fewest since 1985, a reminder that as important as power can be, runs come in sundry ways. Teams can mash, teams can play small ball and teams, like the Brewers, can do it all. They can have coaches with deep reservoirs of hitting wisdom, and they can have vibe guys like Vogelbach, who, as a complement to his technical knowledge, pledged to sing "Stacy's Mom" during the celebration once they left the stadium. They can be serious and excessively regimented, or they can allow for a little fun, like Murphy letting Yelich bring his sweet goldendoodle, Winston, on road trips and give the boys a little respite from the rigors of being the best damn team in the land.

"I don't want to stop playing baseball," Ashby said. "The most special part of this group is that we'll never be this group again, which is so sad."

Here's the thing: Ashby is wrong. The 2026 Milwaukee Brewers are Wisconsin's forever team. Ten years, 25 years, even 50 years from now, they'll be feted wherever they go in the same way Robin Yount and Paul Molitor are still to this day. From Oshkosh to Sheboygan, Eau Claire to Rhinelander, Sturgeon Bay to Stevens Point, they will tell stories of these Brewers, venerate them as unimpeachable heroes. Like Uecker, the man whose voice guided Wisconsinites through thousands of games, they are eternal.

Their new lives started at 11:15 p.m. ET, when Bauers squeezed the final out, and continued amid bubbly and beer -- and wasn't going to stop when they finally showered, changed and headed outside. Awaiting them was a bus. They'd boarded another one three months earlier, and it took them to a magical place. This one was headed to continue the party into the wee hours, and it needed to be christened appropriately. Bauers, Frelick and Woodruff pursed their lips, grabbed rally heaters, lit them and puffed the puffs of fulfilled men. They had won the World Series, just like their captain said they would, and as the bus pulled out of the parking lot at 2:10 a.m. and headed off to the great unknown, the Milwaukee Brewers, champions of the world, were most certainly right.

stories.headline: Love throws 3 TD passes as the Packers beat the Panthers 27-19
stories.summary: — Jordan Love realizes the Green Bay Packers need to finish better.
stories.body:
GREEN BAY, Wis. -- — Jordan Love realizes the Green Bay Packers need to finish better.


They started out well enough Thursday night that their fourth-quarter struggles didn't really matter.


Love threw three touchdown passes, Josh Jacobs scored twice and the Packers withstood three turnovers and Carolina's late comeback attempt to beat the Panthers 27-19.


“Late in the game, it wasn't good enough," Love said. “We weren't able to finish the way we wanted. That's something we've got to improve on, clean up as an offense and be better there.”


Love went 30 of 41 for 288 yards with touchdown passes to Tucker Kraft, Matthew Golden and Jacobs plus an interception. Although Jacobs rushed for only 39 yards on 21 carries against the NFL’s lowest-ranked run defense, he scored on a 4-yard catch and 1-yard run.


That was more than enough for the Packers on a night when they sacked Bryce Young six times. Green Bay hasn't allowed any of its last five opponents to exceed 20 points.


“This defense is really special,” safety Javon Bullard said.


After trailing 27-10 in the third quarter, Carolina cut Green Bay’s lead to 27-19 on Young’s 26-yard touchdown pass to Jalen Coker on a fourth-and-3 play with 5:37 remaining. Young’s ensuing 2-point conversion pass was incomplete.


The Panthers (3-4) got the ball back at their own 45 before losing the ball on downs at midfield with 2:41 remaining. Carolina got one last chance from its own 20 with 22 seconds and no timeouts remaining, but Dani Dennis-Sutton's sack essentially ended any comeback hopes.


“Love the fight in the group,” Panthers coach Dave Canales said. “Didn’t expect anything less. The guys kept battling all the way through, gave us some opportunities at the end.”


Young went 23 of 41 for 209 yards with one touchdown and one interception. Carolina's Chuba Hubbard had 22 carries for 81 yards and a touchdown and seven catches for 38 yards.


Green Bay’s Christian Watson returned to the game after hurting his chest while making a 53-yard catch in the second quarter, causing him to get taken to the hospital. Carolina cornerback Will Lee hurt his hamstring while diving to make a tackle on the same play, and he got carted into the locker room.


Watson said he got clearance to return to the game after a CT scan didn't show any internal bleeding. Watson did say he broke a rib on the play.


“I felt like I was watching ‘WWE Smackdown vs. Raw’ or something, seeing the cameras on me when I was coming out of the ambulance,” said Watson, who caught eight passes for 113 yards. “That was a little crazy. It was a surreal experience, no doubt.”


Carolina already has three other cornerbacks on injured reserve: Akayleb Evans (triceps/knee), Mike Jackson (groin) and Jaycee Horn (quadriceps).


After fumbling the opening kickoff to set up a Carolina field goal and going three-and-out on their first series, the Packers (5-3) scored touchdowns on three of their next four possessions to take command.


Love threw a 12-yard touchdown pass across the middle to Kraft on a third-and-8 play to put Green Bay ahead 6-3, as struggling rookie Trey Smack’s extra-point attempt bounced off the left upright.


Watson’s 53-yard catch set up a Jacobs touchdown run that put Green Bay ahead for good, 13-10 early in the second quarter. One play after dropping a potential touchdown pass, Golden caught a 24-yarder in the left corner of the end zone on third-and-13 to make it 20-10.


Carolina got the ball to start the second half, but Chris McClellan and Evan Williams stopped Hubbard a yard short on fourth-and-2 from midfield. On Green Bay’s ensuing drive, Love found Jacobs to extend the lead to 27-10.


Green Bay led 27-13 and had the ball on Carolina’s 28 in the opening minute of the fourth quarter when Love threw a pass to Golden that Zakee Wheatley intercepted in the end zone.


That turnover sparked Carolina’s comeback attempt, but the Panthers ultimately couldn't break through against Green Bay's defense.


“I said at the beginning of the year, and I still feel this way: I think the sky is the limit for this defense,” Packers linebacker Isaiah McDuffie said.


Brewers get big welcome
Several members of the Milwaukee Brewers, including team captain Christian Yelich and Cy Young Award favorite Jacob Misiorowski, received a huge ovation as they arrived at Lambeau Field one night after winning the first World Series title in franchise history.


Brewers pitcher Brandon Woodruff held the Commissioner’s Trophy aloft as he emerged from the tunnel during a timeout before the second quarter. A few of them attempted a “Lambeau leap” into the crowd, with outfielder Sal Frelick having the most success.


Those Brewers players later were shown on the video board cheering as they wore cheeseheads that included the message, “2026 WS Champions.”


Packers honor Harlan
The Packers honored former president/CEO Bob Harlan during a halftime ceremony in which his name was unveiled on Lambeau Field’s northeast façade alongside that of former Packers general manager Ted Thompson. Harlan, who was the Packers’ president/CEO from 1989-2008, died March 5 at the age of 89.


Injuries
Panthers: OG Corey Bullock hurt his quadriceps in the second half.


Packers: TE Josh Whyle was evaluated for a concussion in the first half.


Up next
Panthers: Host Denver on Nov. 8.


Packers: At New England on Nov. 8.


------

stories.headline: Messi eligible for crunch Miami game with Revs despite yellow card haul
stories.summary: Lionel Messi is eligible for Inter Miami's game against the New England Revolution on Sunday despite receiving his fifth yellow card of the season on Wednesday.
stories.body:
Lionel Messi is eligible for Inter Miami CF's match against the New England Revolution on Sunday despite receiving his fifth yellow card of the season on Wednesday.

Messi received a yellow card in the 44th minute of Miami's 2-2 draw with FC Cincinnati on Wednesday at Nu Stadium, taking his total for the season to five. The Inter Miami captain was also booked during match weeks eight, 11, 20, 31 and 33.

MLS rules state that a player will "automatically reduce his yellow card accumulation total by one yellow card each time he appears in five consecutive matches without receiving a yellow card, red card or supplemental discipline in such matches."

The league's "good behavior incentive" is applied a maximum of three times throughout the regular season.

Messi went more than five games without receiving a yellow card, pardoning his previous yellow card. Though the yellow card will remain on Messi's disciplinary record, the booking no longer counts towards the amount that would force him to face a suspension.

Inter Miami head coach Cristian González said the team no longer has a margin of error when it comes to dropping points during the regular season as they chase Concacaf Champions Cup qualification.

"I am convinced that the frustration we're feeling, much like after the previous match, must make us stronger, because we no longer have any margin for error," González said Wednesday after the draw with Cincinnati. "We need to realize that we are a club that must step up, take risks, be bold, and play football without the fear of making mistakes."

Inter Miami sits in third place in the Eastern Conference, just two points behind the Revs.

Regardless of the outcome, the Herons and Revs have both already qualified for the 2026 MLS playoffs, but Miami's spot in next season's Champions Cup will depend in large part on Sunday's match.

The winners of MLS Cup, the Leagues Cup, U.S. Open Cup, MLS Supporters' Shield and the league's Eastern and Western Conference champions each get a spot in the Champions Cup. With Nashville having secured the Supporters' Shield, second place in the East will get one of the automatic spots, making this penultimate game of the season crucial for the two sides.

stories.headline: Man City, Bayern among the good, bad and lucky in Europe's top leagues
stories.summary: We're a quarter of the way through the 2026-27 European season -- long enough to separate fact from fiction when it comes to from. Who's been lucky? Who's been good? Who's been both, or neither?
stories.body:
About a quarter of the way through the club season, your place in the table only means so much. In the Premier League and Bundesliga, 14 teams -- including Ipswich Town, Paderborn and even Tottenham Hotspur -- are within six points of the top four. In Ligue 1, it's 13. In LaLiga, 14 teams are within six points of the relegation zone. You can find some separation here and there, but we're just getting started, and we only have a partial picture of how things will end up.

We also know that the table is lying a little bit. We see funky results all the time, and they have an outsized impact when we're seen only a small portion of matches. Still, by this point in the 2026-27 campaign, each Big Five team has played hundreds and hundreds of possessions, and we know who is creating (or allowing) the best chances. Thanks to xG, we also know what that means.

Essentially, xG is a chance creation metric. It obviously doesn't guarantee success, especially in the short term, but over the long haul a team's ability to create superior shot quality and/or volume is more predictive than simply who's putting the ball in the net in a small sample. And by comparing who's generated the most points to who's created chance creation advantages, with a fun trend line in between, we can get a grasp of who is ahead of or behind where they should be.

Who's both lucky and good? Who's good, but unlucky? Who's the opposite?

Here are some xG standouts, for better or worse, in Europe's Big Five leagues.

- Jones: Vozinha's Ballon d'Or appearance was made for us

- Ogden: Man United are a mess. Where are the Glazers?

- Olley: Ballon d'Or is Kane's crowning moment

Lucky and good

Definition: Teams with an xG differential of at least +0.3 per game, but more points than expected

Lazio. Lazio have finished seventh or worse in Serie A for three straight years, and due to an ongoing fan protest of club president Claudio Lotito, they're averaging a league-worst home attendance of 9,515. They've also only dropped two points in nine league matches, and they're tied with Inter atop the table. Pretty wild stuff.

It's also probably unsustainable stuff.

While they've enjoyed a few genuinely dominant performances (like a 6-2 win at Sassuolo), they've also scored 22 goals from shots worth just 15.5 xG. Forward Tijjani Noslin, winger Gustav Isaksen and midfielder Kenneth Taylor have combined for nine goals from 3.9 xG; I probably don't have to spell out how unsustainable that is. Lazio have stockpiled enough points to remain in the Champions League hunt for a while, but there's a goal-scoring slump in their future, whether or not there are fans in the stands to see it.

Atletico Madrid. Diego Simeone scoffs at your advanced stats. Over the past 12 full seasons, Atletico have produced a goal differential higher -- and in some cases, much higher -- than their xG differential 11 times. In fact, over the Simeone era, their GD in league play (+504) is 46% higher than their xGD (+346.0). Dark magic is a real thing, I guess.

Atleti have always been happy allowing opponents to hammer shots into a box cluttered by defenders (with the immaculate Jan Oblak behind them), and they've always had impressive finishers -- Antoine Griezmann (143 goals from 113.6 xG) and Angel Correa (68 from 57.4) in particular -- ready to turn a half-chance into a goal. But even without either Griezmann or Correa, they're overachieving again this fall. Oblak remains excellent, Álex Baena has picked up the "major finishing overachiever" mantle, and in four matches with a negative xG differential, Atleti have scored two wins, a draw and only one loss.

Manchester City. No one else has been Lazio-level lucky this season, but City damn near packed a season's worth of xG fortune into one match -- a 5-3 win over Sunderland in which they generated 2.8 xG and allowed 3.6. It was their only match with a negative xG differential this season, but between that and a 1-0 win over Manchester United (xGD: +0.1), they could have easily dropped more points than they actually have this season.

They have an xG cheat code in habitually excellent finisher Erling Haaland (nine goals from shots worth 6.1), but they've been lucky that their defense (seventh in xG allowed) hasn't been more costly.

Borussia Dortmund. It's been difficult to get a read on BVB this season. They've generated a positive xG differential in all seven Bundesliga matches, and their only losses have come against Bayern in the Franz Beckenbauer Super Cup and at Bodø/Glimt in their North Pole fortress in the Champions League. But after winning six straight before the international break, they sandwiched a pair of frustrating draws around the Bodø/Glimt loss upon their return.

Dortmund are on the lucky-and-good list because their defense has been a bit too successful. They've allowed goals in just two Bundesliga matches, and their four goals allowed have come from shots worth 7.3 xG. Yes, they have a high-level goalkeeper in Gregor Kobel, but opponents have simply missed the target quite a bit, too. That likely won't continue, nor will their current tie with Bayern in the league table.

Como. Como are easily Serie A's happiest Champions League story thus far, having won two of their first three matches in their debut in the competition. In theory, they've balanced those duties with solid league play, too -- they're fourth in the league and only five points from first. But they've been at least a little bit fortunate: They've suffered a negative xG differential in four of nine Serie A matches, but they've won two of those four and drawn in one.

- Who are Como? The vacation-destination club that just rocked Man United

That said, the trends are strong: Since returning from the international break, they've suffered a negative xGD only once and have taken 10 points from four league matches. Including their Champions League stomping of Manchester United, they've generated an xGD of at least plus-1.1 in three straight. They were lucky and good, but they might just be good now.

Good, but unlucky

Definition: Teams with an xG differential of at least +0.3 per game and fewer points than expected

Nottingham Forest. If you didn't look at the table, you'd think Oliver Glasner is doing great work in his first season as manager in Nottingham. Forest beat Aston Villa and drew with Liverpool at Anfield, and for the season they're sixth in xG created (13.4), second in xG allowed (9.0) and fifth in overall xG differential. The fundamentals are in great shape.

Somehow they're also 18th in the table, behind even Glasner's direction-less former employer, Crystal Palace. They've turned shots worth 13.4 xG into only six goals; attackers Morgan Gibbs-White, Liam Delap and Chris Wood have attempted 38 shots worth 5.3 xG, but they've put only eight shots on target and scored twice. Forest have generated a positive xG differential in six of eight matches and have somehow won just one of them. That they will almost certainly right the ship in this regard and start winning matches soon, but how many unnecessary points will they have dropped by then?

Brest. After surging to third in Ligue 1 in 2023-24 and qualifying for the Champions League, Brest slipped to ninth and then 12th in the last two seasons. Now they're 13th. It appears the balloon is losing helium.

If the results start matching the chance creation, however, a turnaround is possible. They're second in Ligue 1 in xG differential, well behind PSG but well ahead of everyone else. They've created a dominant xG differential of +1.9 or better in four matches but have somehow won only one of them. Both their finishing and defense have let them down at times, but midfielder Joris Chotard is fifth in the league in chances created, and the combo of young wingers Kamory Doumbia and Pathé Mboup with veteran big man Ludovic Ajorque has created a number of dangerous opportunities.

This is one of France's better teams, no matter what the table says.

Villarreal. Villarreal are third in xG differential and 10th in LaLiga. They have dropped unlikely points to Atletico Madrid (2-2 draw, +2.8 xG differential), Elche (0-0 draw, +2.1 xGD) and Alaves (1-0 loss, +1.0). Forwards Georges Mikautadze and Ayoze Pérez have scored just four goals from shots worth 8.4 xG; in the Champions League, meanwhile, they've scored two goals from 1.2.

Aside from finishing, there's nothing inherently wrong with this squad. They're third in shots per possession margin and fourth in xG per shot margin. They play a pretty possession game -- Renato Veiga is one of only two players in LaLiga (along with Barcelona's Gerard Martín) to already have over 100 progressive passes and 100 progressive carries -- without giving up much on the counter. But they're eight points behind fourth-place Real Betis; they have some ground to make up.

Bournemouth. Only Manchester City, Arsenal and Brentford have led more Premier League matches this season than Bournemouth, but somehow the Cherries have turned leads in six matches -- and positive xG differentials in six matches -- into just two wins. Marcus Tavernier has scored a lovely five goals from shots worth 3.6 xG, but the rest of the team has just six goals from shots worth 10.9. They aren't generating the sizable advantages they should, and they've been outscored 4-0 from the 80th minute on. They're third in xG differential but 13th in the table because of the late leaks.

It could be worse -- most of their unfortunate results have been draws and not losses. But with so many bigger clubs struggling out of the gate, Bournemouth had a chance to establish a good spot in the race for a top-five finish. They're off of that pace.

Bayern Munich. Maybe one day this hard-luck club will catch a break. Alas, the 35-time German champions have dropped points twice -- 0-0 at Schalke (xG differential: +1.7), 2-2 at Augsburg (+2.5) -- despite dominating the early stages of the season as much as ever.

Seriously, though, this is ridiculous:

Every so often, the Bundesliga figures out how to balance great crowds, fun stories and sustained challenges for Bayern, but it doesn't appear this will be one of those years, even if those two draws mean Bayern and Borussia Dortmund are tied in points at the moment. Bayern's xGD is actually higher now than it was after they won their first seven matches last season.

Ballon d'Or winner (!) Harry Kane has gone through his version of a finishing funk (he has four league goals from shots worth 5.2 xG), and Serge Gnabry is in a similar boat (one goal from 2.2 xG). Something tells me they'll be all right.

Bad, but unlucky

Definition: Teams with an xG differential worse than minus-0.3 per game and fewer points than expected

Venezia. It's a yo-yo period in Venice. Venezia were promoted from Serie B in 2021, but went straight back down. They came back up in 2024, went back down in 2025, then came right back up in 2026. And through eight matchdays, they have three points and are last in the Serie A table.

However, they haven't been that bad. This team obviously isn't loaded with proven finishers, but scoring just six goals from shots worth 14.5 xG is severely unfortunate. Forwards John Yeboah, Albion Rrahmani and Lion Lauberbach somehow have one goal from 5.1 xG; they aren't generating ridiculously high-quality shots, but that is still some unsustainably poor finishing. Venezia have generated a positive xG differential in four of nine matches, and they're 14th overall in xGD. They'll have a chance to stay up if their finishing begins to reflect their actual chance creation.

Borussia Mönchengladbach. The five-time German champions finally notched a win last weekend, shocking Stuttgart 3-2. It was both deserving and a long time coming. They had lost their first six league matches, alternating between awful (losing to RB Leipzig and Freiburg by a combined 8-0) and unlucky (4-3 losses to Elversberg and Mainz despite a combined xGD of +0.5).

The club hired former St. Pauli manager Alexander Blessin on Sept. 22, and while he made an immediate impact on their defense, they finally generated some offense in Stuttgart too. American right midfielder Joe Scally and 17-year old left midfielder Wael Mohya each had a goal and an assist in that match, and if Gladbach can generate production like that from the wings, maybe it will offset the black hole of production they've gotten from their center forwards in the absence of injured veteran Tim Kleindienst.

Valencia. After pulling nine points from their first 11 league matches last year and 10 from their first 15 in 2024-25, Valencia have just six points after 10 matches this season. Only Villarreal and Osasuna have been worse at finishing the season: Valencia have turned shots worth 10.8 xG into only seven goals. In matches against Real Betis (1-0 loss), Celta Vigo (0-0 draw) and Athletic Club (0-0 draw) they attempted 40 shots worth 3.3 xG, and none went in the net. Those matches could have easily produced six to nine points ... but yielded just two instead.

Despite average defensive numbers, there's no way to say this team is anything better than below average. But while they're growing awfully familiar to relegation scraps at the moment -- and if you play with fire enough, you will get burned -- I can't say they're actually relegation-worthy just yet.

Troyes. Back in Ligue 1 after a three-year absence, Troyes attempt more shots than their opponents and press frequently. They don't attempt many good shots, but they rank 15th in xG created and 10th in xG allowed. That they only have five points from eight matches is therefore a smidgen unlucky. They've scored only five goals from shots worth 9.7 xG, and they've allowed 16 goals from shots worth 13.2. A lot of that damage comes from one match -- a 6-2 loss to Strasbourg in which both teams generated 2.9 xG -- but forwards Renaud Ripart and Jeremy Le Douaron have combined for two goals on 4.7 xG. Finish at more normal levels, and they'll have a solid shot at survival.

Sunderland. Sunderland were the "stats don't matter" team of 2025-26, ranking 18th in the Premier League in xG differential, but somehow finishing seventh and grabbing a spot in the Europa League. You usually don't have to wait long for what we'll call statistical comeuppance. This year they've actually improved to 15th in xG differential, and they've generated a positive xGD in four of eight matches, but they've won just one because aside from Brian Brobbey (three goals from shots worth 3.2 xG), no one can turn shots into goals.

Sunderland rank third in the league in xG per shot, but they're 18th in goals and haven't scored in a league match since Sept. 20. That puts them at the bottom of the table. A lot of teams are struggling at the moment, so they're not in too big a hole, but after this weekend's trip to Coventry City, their schedule gets awfully tricky.

Lucky and bad

Definition: Teams with an xG differential worse than minus-0.3 per game but more points than expected

Frosinone. Frosinone have been promoted to Serie A four times since 2015; they have yet to avoid going straight back down. That they're currently sixth in points per game, ahead of mighty Juventus, is a thrilling story. But it's really hard to believe this story will last. They're also 18th in xG differential, having scored 17 goals from shots worth 13.1 xG while allowing 13 goals from shots worth 19.5.

This is unsustainable in obvious ways, but as Sunderland learned last year, if you stockpile points early, you can ride it out when regression to the mean invariably hits. They're already nine points above the drop zone with a game in hand; from here, it won't take too much additional good fortune for them to survive a year in Serie A for the first time.

Elversberg. The most delightful early Bundesliga story is also a fortunate one. Tiny Elversberg, from a town of 13,000 people, have three wins and 10 points from seven matches in their top-division debut. They're a healthy eighth in the table, but they also have yet to actually generate a positive xG differential in a match, and in three one-goal wins they scored 11 goals from shots worth 7.4 xG.

This is an optimistic team with fun attacking ideas, and maybe they can continue to avoid the relegation hunt with bursts of excellence from players such as 22-year-old David Mokwa (1.2 xG, two goals) and 21-year-old Maurice Krattenmacher (2.4 xG, three goals). But they lost 4-0 to RB Leipzig last weekend, and it feels like there might be a few more heavy defeats in their future. Hopefully I'm wrong.

Marseille. Not only are Marseille a terribly disappointing eighth in Ligue 1 at the moment, but they're lucky to even be that high. Their 18 goals scored (first in the league) have come from just 13.6 xG (seventh), while their 18.5 xG allowed (last) has turned into only 13 goals (11th). Last week's 4-3 win over Le Havre featured a minus-1.6 xG differential.

Only Strasbourg have a lower league xG differential than l'OM right now. Marseille do have historically solid finishers like Amine Gouiri and Igor Paixão pacing the attack, and a lot of their defensive overachievement came from a single match -- a 2-1 loss to PSG in which they allowed shots worth 5.1 xG. Still, the fundamentals do not suggest that manager Bruno Genesio is fielding a team worth a spot in a European competition at the moment.

Cagliari. Like Frosinone, Cagliari has stocked up on some early points (13 in nine Serie A matches) thanks to some early good fortune. They've suffered a negative xG differential in six of nine matches, but have won two of those with a draw. They've gotten spectacular goalkeeping from Elia Caprile thus far, but allowing just 13 goals from shots worth 17.3 xG is pretty fortunate.

Strangely, though, it's offset some poor finishing from Cagliari, too: While left winger Daniel Maldini is on a hot streak (five goals from shots worth 3.4 xG), the rest of the team has just three goals from 8.1 xG, and if their own finishing progresses more than opponents', they could remain mid-table for quite a while longer.

Newcastle United. Let's isolate that PPG vs. xGD chart above with just Premier League teams.

Maybe no attack in Europe has defied xG more than Newcastle's, and in two different directions.

- Yoane Wissa: 1 goal from shots worth 3.0 xG (minus-2.0 difference)

- Everyone else: 11 goals from shots worth 6.2 xG (plus-4.8 difference)

Wissa has done a great job of generating nearly one-third of Newcastle's xG by himself, but he's been in a major finishing slump. And it's been more than offset by the fact that other guys can't seem to miss.

Newcastle ranks 16th in shots per possession margin and 19th in xG per shot margin; they've generated a positive xG differential in only one match, but incredibly, they lost that match and have only lost two of seven with a negative xGD. It either works (two of three wins were by two goals) or really, really doesn't (two of three losses were by three goals). And I honestly don't have much of an idea of what to expect from them moving forward. I'm not incredibly optimistic, though.

stories.headline: AFL 2027 fixture: Five must-watch games in the first month
stories.summary: The 2027 AFL fixture has been released. So, to whet your appetite for the upcoming season, we've picked out the five must-watch games from the opening month.
stories.body:
The 2027 AFL fixture has been released. So, to whet your appetite for the upcoming season, we've picked out the five must-watch games from the opening month of action.

Get the popcorn ready and get set to enjoy these absolute belters in the new year.

5. Port Adelaide vs. Western Bulldogs - Round 4, Adelaide Oval, Sunday, April 8, 7:40pm (AEDT)
Make no mistake, when Zak Butters returns to Adelaide Oval to face his old mob for the first time since departing, it's going to be incredibly spicy.

In a move that shocked absolutely nobody, Butters left Port Adelaide during the 2026 trade period, inking a long-term deal with the Western Bulldogs. It's a brutal blow for the Power, and his ex-teammates will be sure to give him a hard time when they share the field in Round 4. You just know it's going to be on for young and old!

The AFL also made the move to schedule this blockbuster game as the closer to next year's Gather Round. It means far more bodies will be in Adelaide that weekend and a greater number of eyeballs on the clash.

4. Hawthorn vs. Geelong - Round 2, MCG, Monday, March 29, 3:15pm (AEDT)
The traditional Easter Monday clash between the Hawks and Cats is always on our shortlist of early season must-watch games, and next year will be no exception.

Both of these clubs are in the premiership window. Both clubs have added high-profile players this offseason. Both clubs have fanbases that bring an electric energy to Easter Monday at the MCG.

This one is also set to be a fascinating coaching battle between Chris Scott and Sam Mitchell, two of the game's best tacticians, who will go head-to-head just as much as the players on the field.

3. Fremantle vs. Western Bulldogs - Round 1, Optus Stadium, Thursday, March 18, 8:10pm (AEDT)
This Round 1 game in the west is simply oozing with intrigue.

Of course, the question on everyone's mind is how the Dockers back up after having this year's premiership ripped away from them in harrowing circumstances. Does it galvanise the club? Will we see 'Wharfie Time'? Surely not!

For the Bulldogs, they landed the biggest fish of the off-season in superstar midfielder Zak Butters. This will be the first opportunity to watch him play in his new colours, lining up in the middle alongside skipper Marcus Bontempelli and Ed Richards.

2. Brisbane vs. Collingwood - Round 2, Gabba, Thursday, March 25, 7:50pm (AEDT)
Reigning premier Brisbane will unfurl its latest flag in Round 2 when it hosts Collingwood in its first home game of the season, a clash that has blockbuster written all over it.

The Lions are looking to become just the second team ever to win four consecutive flags (joining, you guessed it, Collingwood from 1927 to 1930) but will be doing it without superstar midfielder Lachie Neale. The two-time Brownlow medallist departed for the Magpies this offseason, making this early season contest between the two clubs extra intriguing.

Plus, any opportunity to watch current Brownlow medallist Nick Daicos play footy is reason in itself to tune in!

1. Hawthorn vs. Brisbane - Round 1, MCG, Friday, March 19, 7:40pm (AEDT)
Thankfully we don't have to wait long for the Hawks and Lions -- quite possibly the competition's two best teams -- to square off in 2027. And if this game delivers even 70% of what these sides dished up in this year's epic preliminary final, then we're in for an absolute treat!

Many have labelled Brisbane's thrilling win over Hawthorn this past September as the greatest game of footy played this century. That in itself should be enough of a reason for their next clash to simply be must-watch.

There will be extra intrigue with both teams given this clash falls in Round 1. For the Lions, they will be looking to navigate life without both superstar midfielder Lachie Neale and master coach Chris Fagan, while the Hawks will be attempting to integrate recruits Zach Merrett and Ben King into their line-up.

stories.headline: It's still the age of Volkanovski in MMA pound-for-pound rankings
stories.summary: At age 38, UFC featherweight champion makes big jump in ESPN's P4P top 10.
stories.body:
Alexander Volkanovski made a bold statement at UFC 333 that, even at age 38, he isn't ready to surrender his place among the greatest in MMA. The ESPN pound-for-pound voting panel took note.

On the strength of Volkanovski's second-round knockout of previously undefeated Movsar Evloev on Saturday, the UFC featherweight champion makes a big jump in the latest men's rankings. Volkanovski is No. 2, after entering the weekend five positions lower.

Volkanovski was so impressive that he outshined the co-main event performance of Petr Yan, who defended the men's bantamweight title by beating former champion Merab Dvalishvili. Yan drops one spot to No. 3, the position Dvalishvili used to occupy. Dvalishvili is now tied for eighth after his second straight loss to Yan in their fiery trilogy.

The other significant change near the top of the rankings is the disappearance of Tom Aspinall. The former UFC heavyweight champion is still healing from eye injuries suffered in a no-contest against Ciryl Gane in October 2025. Because Aspinall has not fought in over a year, he is ineligible for the rankings.

For the ESPN divisional MMA rankings, click here.

Note: Results are current; rankings are as of Oct. 28. To be eligible for the rankings, a fighter must have competed over the past 12 months or must have an upcoming fight booked. Fighters who have been dropped for inactivity can be reinstated only after they compete.

Men's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Islam Makhachev

UFC welterweight champion

Record: 29-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Ian Machado Garry, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Makhachev vacated the UFC lightweight championship to go for a second title at welterweight. By winning that belt last November with a thrashing of Jack Della Maddalena, Makhachev staked his place among MMA's greatest -- not just in today's sport but of all time. His win over Machado Garry at UFC 330 was his 17th straight, breaking the UFC record for consecutive wins. Makhachev is piling up unprecedented achievements.

2. Alexander Volkanovski

UFC featherweight champion

Previous ranking: 7

Record: 29-4

Last: W (TKO2) vs. Movsar Evloev, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

It felt as if the sport had started to write Volkanovski's eulogy following his knockout loss to Ilia Topuria in February 2024. Volkanovski noticed and made a point of proving to everyone he still has plenty left by recapturing the featherweight belt at UFC 314, the first of two consecutive wins over Lopes. His age (38) will likely continue to be a prefight topic, which is fine because Volkanovski enjoys proving people wrong. He did just that by handing Evloev his first loss at UFC 333.

3. Petr Yan

UFC bantamweight champion

Previous ranking: 2

Record: 21-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Merab Dvalishvili, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

What a return to the top it's been for Yan. He began his career with 15 consecutive wins before going on a 1-4 run from 2021 to 2023. That almost doesn't feel real now, after watching him reclaim his throne against Dvalishvili, who once handed him the worst loss of his career, then completing his trilogy with Dvalishvili with a successful title defense. Yan took a major detour, but this was the destination we felt he was capable of before the skid. He once again looks like one of the best fighters on the planet.

4. Ilia Topuria

UFC lightweight

Previous ranking: 6

Record: 17-1

Last: L (TKO4) vs. Justin Gaethje, June 14

Next: TBA

Topuria was an undefeated two-division champion when he ran into Gaethje at UFC Freedom 250 and was brutalized in a stoppage loss. How will that affect the immediate future of Topuria? His knockout wins over two of the greatest featherweights, Alexander Volkanovski and Max Holloway, gave him an intimidating aura. Can the former champion get that back?

5. Justin Gaethje

UFC lightweight champion

Previous ranking: Tied for 4

Record: 28-5

Last: W (TKO4) vs. Ilia Topuria, June 14

Next: TBA

Gaethje has spent his 15-year career thrilling MMA fans, but before the title bout on the White House lawn, all he had to show for it -- aside from 15 bonus checks in 15 UFC appearances -- were two missed opportunities to be an undisputed champion. His fourth-round TKO of Topuria got Gaethje over the hump. It was a resilient performance in a back-and-forth battle that is a prime candidate for fight of the year. More important for Gaethje: At age 37, he is finally sitting at the top of the mountain.

6. Joshua Van

UFC flyweight champion

Previous ranking: 8

Record: 18-2

Last: W (UD) vs. Alexandre Pantoja, Sept. 19

Next: Jan. 30 vs. Manel Kape

Van has been champion since December, but until UFC 331, there were doubters. Van had been handed the belt by default, when his challenge for the title was waved off after 26 seconds because Pantoja dislocated his left elbow. Van went on to defend the title against Tatsuro Taira in May, then faced Pantoja in a rematch at UFC 331. Van produced a clear victory -- his eighth win in a row -- to leave no doubt who rules at 125 pounds.

7. Arman Tsarukyan

UFC lightweight

Previous ranking: 10

Record: 24-3

Last: W (KO1) vs. Mauricio Ruffy, Sept. 19

Next: TBA

Tsarukyan is right back in the place he was in January 2025 -- on the cusp of a title fight. He withdrew from a challenge of Islam Makhachev one day before UFC 311 because of a back injury, and later in the year he was passed over twice when the UFC was booking lightweight title bouts. But by knocking out Ruffy with an elbow in the first round at UFC 331, Tsarukyan put himself back at the front of the line.

T-8. Merab Dvalishvili

UFC bantamweight

Previous ranking: 3

Record: 21-6

Last: L (UD) vs. Petr Yan, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

Dvalishvili was on one of the most impressive runs through the UFC's bantamweight division ever. Not only did he defeat Sean O'Malley for the second time in nine months at UFC 316, but he showcased a new part of his game, finishing O'Malley with a guillotine. Starting in August 2022, Dvalishvili beat José Aldo, Yan, Henry Cejudo, O'Malley (twice), Umar Nurmagomedov and Cory Sandhagen. But at UFC 323, in an attempt to become the first champion in UFC history to successfully defend a title four times in a calendar year, Dvalishvili lost a rematch with Yan. Their third meeting at UFC 333 was the most competitive in their trilogy, but Dvalishvili fell short again.

T-8. Ciryl Gane

UFC heavyweight champion

Previous ranking: 9

Record: 14-2, 1 NC

Last: W (TKO2) vs. Alex Pereira, June 14

Next: Nov. 14 vs. Josh Hokit

Gane is unique in that he is the first -- and could very well go down as the only -- heavyweight to face the division's four biggest names in Francis Ngannou, Jon Jones, Tom Aspinall and Pereira. None of those four have fought each other, yet all four have have fought the Frenchman. Gane was 0-2 with a no-contest against that group before he knocked out Pereira in the second round of their interim title fight on the White House lawn. Gane was elevated to undisputed champ after Aspinall, still injured, vacated his title, and the new champ will defend against Hokit at UFC 334.

10. Alex Pereira

UFC heavyweight

Previous ranking: Unranked

Record: 13-4

Last: L (TKO2) vs. Ciryl Gane, June 14

Next: Dec. 12 vs. Sergei Pavlovich

Pereira made a big splash in the MMA after a world championship career in kickboxing. He joined the UFC in 2021 and became a middleweight champion the following year, then moved on to be a two-time light heavyweight titlist before making an unprecedented bid for a belt in a third weight class when he fought Game at UFC Freedom 250 for an interim heavyweight title. Pereira got knocked out in that fight, but now he's back on his feet and in position to reclaim his position when he faces a fellow title contender, Pavlovich, at UFC 335.

Other fighters receiving votes: Alexandre Pantoja and Sean Strickland.

How our panel voted
Brett Okamoto: 1. Islam Makhachev; 2. Petr Yan; 3. Ilia Topuria; 4. Alexander Volkanovski; 5. Joshua Van; 6. Arman Tsarukyan; 7. Merab Dvalishvili; 8. Ciryl Gane; 9. Alex Pereira; 10. Justin Gaethje.

Carlos Contreras Legaspi: 1. Makhachev; 2. Volkanovski; 3. Gaethje; 4. Topuria; 5. Yan; 6. Van; 7. Pereira; 8. Dvalishvili; 9. Gane; 10. Tsarukyan.

Andrew Davis: 1. Makhachev; 2. Volkanovski; 3. Yan; 4. Gaethje; 5. Topuria; 6. Van; 7. Gane; 8. Tsarukyan; 9 Pereira; 10. Sean Strickland.

Dre Waters: 1. Makhachev; 2. Volkanovski; 3. Yan; 4. Gaethje; 5. Topuria; 6. Van; 7. Dvalishvili; 8. Gane; 9. Pereira; 10. Tsarukyan.

Jeff Wagenheim: 1. Makhachev; 2. Yan; 3. Volkanovski; 4. Van; 5. Gaethje; 6. Tsarukyan; 7. Topuria; 8. Dvalishvili; 9. Gane; 10. Alexandre Pantoja.

Women's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Valentina Shevchenko

UFC flyweight

Record: 26-4-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Zhang Weili, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

Shevchenko's dominance came under question in 2022 and 2023, when she went 1-1-1 in a trilogy with Alexa Grasso. Boy, does that feel like a long time ago now. Shevchenko more than reasserted herself as the best flyweight in the world, and then she established herself as the No. 1 woman in the world, period. It wasn't surprising that she beat Zhang, but it was surprising how easy she made it look. Shevchenko is out injured, however, so she has vacated her UFC title, which Natalia Silva captured by beating Wang Cong at UFC 332. When Shevchenko is healed up, she'll be looking to take back the belt.

2. Zhang Weili

UFC flyweight / strawweight

Record: 26-4

Last: L (UD) vs. Valentina Shevchenko, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

It's hard to move up in weight, especially at the highest level. That sounds like it should be obvious, but Zhang had been dominant at 115 pounds for so long, some of us might have taken for granted how big of a challenge moving to 125 would be. UFC 322 was a bad night for Zhang, but she doesn't have many. And if she decides to stay at flyweight, it certainly seems reasonable to believe she'll fare better in the future.

3. Cris Cyborg

PFL featherweight champion

Record: 30-2, 1 NC

Last: W (UD) vs. Ketlen Vieira, Aug. 22

Next: TBA

It had been a while since Cyborg had fought an elite opponent in MMA until she met Larissa Pacheco in 2024. That was a legitimate matchup -- and many within the industry were predicting Cyborg's downfall. Instead, she took out the PFL's two-weight champion, upending all of Pacheco's momentum. One of the original pioneers of women's MMA is once again a champion after getting her second career submission at PFL Lyon in December. The PFL promoted her fight with Vieira as a retirement bout, but after her win Cyborg did not sound like someone who is done fighting.

4. Natalia Silva

UFC flyweight champion

Record: 21-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Wang Cong, Oct. 3

Next: TBA

Silva was looking every bit the part of a future UFC champion following a dominant display against Alexa Grasso at UFC 315 and a victory over Rose Namajunas at UFC 324. And now she has fulfilled that expectation, beating Wang at UFC 332 to win the belt vacated by injured Valentina Shevchenko. Silva's stick-and-move style has frustrated even the highest level of opponent, and she's got youth on her side as she won't turn 30 until 2027.

5. Mackenzie Dern

UFC strawweight champion

Record: 17-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Gillian Robertson, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Dern's rise to the 115-pound throne was truly a changing of the guard. She is the division's first first-time champion since 2019, because the previous three champs -- Zhang Weili, Carla Esparza and Rose Namajunas -- all were in their second reigns. Dern, nearly a decade into her MMA career after multiple jiu-jitsu world championships, has won four fights in a row, including a dominant performance against a fellow grappling-heavy fighter, Robertson, in her first title defense.

6. Alexa Grasso

UFC flyweight

Record: 18-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Manon Fiorot, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Grasso went nearly three years without winning a fight, but her 2023 win right before the skid was a huge one, a submission of Valentina Shevchenko for the UFC title. What followed were two more fights with Shevchenko -- a draw, then a loss -- and then a loss to Natalia Silva. But she reasserted herself with a finish of Maycee Barber in March, then got the best of Fiorot, a fellow title contender, at Noche UFC to put herself in position for another title shot.

7. Dakota Ditcheva

PFL flyweight

Record: 16-0

Last: W (UD) vs. Denise Kielholtz, July 31

Next: TBA

Not only did Ditcheva win the PFL's flyweight season in 2024, but she did so in spectacular fashion -- a TKO finish over Taila Santos, who once challenged for a UFC title. Ditcheva fought only once in 2025, dominating Sumiko Inaba in the co-main event of the first PFL Champions Series card in Cape Town, South Africa. She then spent over a year on the sideline, healing injuries to both hands, before returning at PFL New York with a dominant win over Kielholtz.

8. Manon Fiorot

UFC flyweight

Record: 13-3

Last: L (UD) vs. Alexa Grasso, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Fiorot had handled everyone the UFC put in front of her -- except the champion, Valentina Shevchenko, who defeated the Frenchwoman at UFC 315 in May 2025. But then, with another title shot within her grasp, Fiorot ran into Grasso, a former champion, at Noche UFC and lost a competitive fight.

9. Tatiana Suarez

UFC strawweight

Record: 12-1

Last: W (Sub2) vs. Loopy Godínez, April 11

Next: Nov. 7 vs. Virna Jandiroba

If Suarez is still feeling the effects of last year's humbling defeat to Zhang Weili in a title challenge, she certainly didn't show it at UFC 327, overcoming early adversity to thrash Godinez, a fellow top-10 strawweight. Suarez is going to be a tough out for anyone at 115 pounds.

10. Virna Jandiroba

UFC strawweight

Record: 23-4

Last: W (UD) vs. Tabatha Ricci, April 4

Next: Nov. 7 vs. Tatiana Suarez

Jandiroba fell short in last October's fight with Mackenzie Dern for the vacant title, but she bounced back in April with a victory over Ricci. Up next is a top-10 showdown with Suarez, who also lost a title challenge last year. The winner will be right back in the championship mix.

Other fighter receiving votes: Joselyne Edwards and Jasmine Jasudavicius.
