stories.headline: NRL transfer whispers: Sua Fa'alogo agrees to long-term Storm extension
stories.summary: The NRL season may be over, but the player market is already heating up ahead of November 1. Isaac Issa has news on Bradman Best's future and which clubs might be lining up a play for Sam Walker.
stories.body:
The NRL season may be over, but the player market is already heating up ahead of November 1, with clubs beginning to shape their rosters for 2027 and beyond.

From player movement to changes behind the scenes, ESPN NRL Insider Isaac Issa has the latest whispers from around the competition.

Fa'alogo agrees to long-term Storm extension

Sua Fa'alogo has agreed to extend his stay at the Melbourne Storm through to the end of 2032, ESPN understands.

The agreement will keep the fullback in Melbourne for the next six seasons, securing a key figure in the Storm's long-term plans.

Fa'alogo's retention delivers a major boost for Melbourne ahead of the November 1 contracting window, with the club moving to lock down one of its most exciting talents.

Dolphins close in on Lemuelu extension, confident of keeping Farnworth

The Dolphins are closing in on a multi-year extension for Connelly Lemuelu as they also express confidence in retaining Herbie Farnworth.

ESPN understands Lemuelu is nearing an agreement to extend his stay despite interest from Canberra, Parramatta and Cronulla.

Securing the back-rower would deliver a retention boost for the Dolphins, with the length of the proposed deal yet to be confirmed.

The club is also understood to be confident it can retain Farnworth despite links to the Sydney Roosters.

While that confidence is yet to translate into a confirmed extension, keeping the English international alongside Lemuelu would help preserve key combinations on the Dolphins' left edge.

Eels edge ahead in Best race
Parramatta have emerged as the frontrunners to land Bradman Best, with multiple sources indicating the Newcastle centre is increasingly likely to join the Eels beyond 2027.

Best has been identified as a priority target for Parramatta, who are looking to bolster Jason Ryles' backline with an established representative star.

While a deal is yet to be confirmed, the Eels are understood to be in the box seat despite Newcastle's efforts to retain him with a lucrative extension.

Bulldogs unlikely to enter Walker race
Canterbury are unlikely to enter the race for Sam Walker, with the Bulldogs backing their existing halfback options ahead of the upcoming season.

Despite suggestions the club could emerge as a potential destination for Walker, it is understood Canterbury are taking a wait-and-see approach rather than preparing to launch a pursuit.

The Bulldogs' immediate focus remains on the internal battle for the No.7 jersey, with Mitch and Alex Conti set to compete for the role over the offseason.

Canterbury have not completely shut the door on a move should circumstances change, but their current position suggests they are unlikely to become an active contender for Walker's signature.

For now, the Bulldogs are content to watch how the situation unfolds.

stories.headline: How Kimi Antonelli can win F1 title at Mexico City GP -- with or without Qatar, Abu Dhabi races
stories.summary: Kimi Antonelli took another big step towards his first world title after outscoring his two closest championship rivals, George Russell and Lewis Hamilton, at the Singapore Grand Prix.
stories.body:
Kimi Antonelli inched closer to his first world title after extending his lead in the championship from his two closest rivals George Russell and Lewis Hamilton, at the United States Grand Prix.

The 20-year-old, who has the potential to set a new record for the youngest Formula 1 champion this year, now leads Mercedes teammate Russell by a whopping 123 points in the standings with a maximum of 100 points still up for grabs.

The substantial lead means he is looking more than likely to be crowned champion on Nov. 1 at the Mexico City Grand Prix. The grands prix in Qatar and Abu Dhabi are currently scheduled to go ahead on Nov. 29 and Dec. 6, but escalations in the war between the United States and Iran have the potential to force the cancellation of both rounds.

F1 has put a contingency plan in place to hold a single round at Imola if Qatar and Abu Dhabi are cancelled, but doing so would cut the championship short by one round and mean only 75 points are available to any single driver before the end of the year. Such a scenario would mean Antonelli has already won the title after maximising all the points on offer in Austin.

- Kimi Antonelli wins United States GP but made to wait for first F1 title

- Toto Wolff hails Kimi Antonelli on U.S GP win: 'The race of a champion who isn't a champion yet'

- George Russell: Finishing second in F1 title race 'doesn't mean anything'

Max Verstappen, Charles Leclerc and Lando Norris were in mathematical contention for this year's championship, but after Austin, they are no longer in the title fight, leaving just Russell and Hamilton still in the mix.

What does Antonelli need to do to be crowned champion in Mexico?
Assuming the final two races go ahead as planned, Antonelli's chances of clinching the title in Mexico have now dramatically increased after he converted his Mercedes from pole into his ninth race victory of the season in Austin. Antonelli would need to finish in ninth place or higher in Mexico to be crowned champion, even if Russell wins the race.

If Hamilton wins in Mexico, a 10th place finish for Antonelli would be enough for him to seal the title. Antonelli needs to score two points, or not be outscored by Russell by 24 points and Hamilton by 25 points. If neither Russell or Hamilton win the race, Antonelli will win the championship regardless of where he finishes.

If Russell did win and Antonelli finished below ninth, the gap between them would be 99 points with 100 points remaining, but even if Antonelli failed to score another point and Russell won all the remaining rounds after Mexico, Antonelli would still be crowned champion on countback of race victories.

If the championship is shortened by the season ending in Imola rather than Abu Dhabi, Antonelli has already become world champion in Austin, but the final races are still due to go ahead as planned.

The permutations for Antonelli to be crowned champion in Mexico City are:

If Antonelli finishes ninth or higher, he will be crowned champion regardless of where the others finish and even if Russell wins the race.
If Antonelli finishes tenth, he would be crowned champion even if Hamilton wins the race.
If Hamilton or Russell don't win the race, Antonelli will be crowned champion no matter where he finishes.

What's the minimum Antonelli needs to do be crowned champion?
Another way to look at the championship is the minimum amount of points Antonelli needs to score over the remaining rounds to secure the title regardless of what other drivers achieve. Assuming Qatar and Abu Dhabi go ahead, he needs just two points over the remaining rounds.

stories.headline: Valkyries focused on positives after Game 6 loss to Dream
stories.summary: Their approach after a disastrous first quarter Thursday is something the Valkyries can take home for the deciding Game 7 against the Dream on Saturday.
stories.body:
ATLANTA -- The first quarter Thursday was a disaster for the Golden State Valkyries. But Game 6 of the WNBA Finals wasn't a complete wash, point guard Veronica Burton said.

"I'm sitting here and the body language is bad," Burton said after Golden State fell 80-69 to the Atlanta Dream, tying the series at 3-all. "But at the end of the day, we feel good. Yes, we lost. Yes, it was a bad game for us. We had a terrible first quarter. [But] we cleaned it up. We found a way. We didn't quit. Games 2 and 3 were ugly, and we quit. We looked bad. And we didn't quit on this one."

The Valkyries were able to trim an Atlanta lead that reached 25 down to eight in the fourth quarter. That's something to take back home with them for the deciding Game 7 on Saturday in San Francisco.

"It is do-or-die, officially," Burton said of the mentality both teams must have Saturday.

The Dream were in that position Thursday, too, down 3-2 in the series. The Valkyries spoke Wednesday about needing to match the sense of desperation and urgency they knew the Dream would have in Game 6. As is so often the case in best-of-seven series in any sport, the team with its back against the wall played with more ferocity.

After holding Atlanta to just 55 points Monday in Game 5's victory, the Valkyries allowed the Dream to score 32 in the first quarter Thursday.

Everything that looked so difficult offensively for the Dream in Games 1, 4 and 5 appeared much easier in Game 6, to the delight of the sold-out matinee crowd at State Farm Arena.

The game began at 12:30 p.m. local time, which was 9:30 a.m. Pacific time, but the Valkyries players and coaches dismissed fatigue and the early start time -- "They played at the same time as us, right?" Golden State's Gabby Williams said -- as factors in their slow start.

"Just frustrated," Golden State coach Natalie Nakase said. "It's unacceptable."

The Dream were sharper with their ball movement and made open shots, something they had struggled to do at times earlier in the series. Atlanta's 32-15 advantage after the first quarter was just too much for the defense-oriented Valkyries to make up.

But as Burton said, they didn't throw in the towel. The rest of the game was closer. Atlanta outscored Golden State by just three points in the second quarter. Then in the second half, the Valkyries actually "won" both quarters, by four points in the third and five in the fourth.

Burton referenced the Valkyries' 79-65 loss in Game 2 at San Francisco and their 97-71 loss in Game 3 in Atlanta as games in which the Valkyries stopped battling to win. That didn't happen Thursday, which meant the Dream still had to play all their starters at least 30 minutes.

Thursday was also just the second time in the series that the Dream shot better than 40% from the field. They finished at 44% Thursday and were at 49% in Game 3 on Oct. 21.

Williams finished with 26 points and Tiffany Hayes 15 for the Valkyries. Golden State wanted to be close in the rebounding battle and was, winning it 36-35. The Valkyries also had just 10 turnovers to the Dream's 15. Those are the good things that Burton and her team will focus on as they prepare for the last game of the 2026 season.

"We didn't give ourselves a good position at the start of the game, but we feel good, and there's a lot to take away from the second, third and fourth quarters," Burton said. "Our defense was a little more like us [in the second half], so we'll watch that, see the adjustments they made, see where we can adjust, and I think we're in a good spot."

stories.headline: Cavan Sullivan turned 17 last month, but he's already playing like an MLS MVP
stories.summary: Since MLS resumed after the World Cup, Cavan Sullivan has been the league's best player not named Lionel Messi. Does he deserve some MVP recognition?
stories.body:
Philadelphia Union interim manager Ryan Richter remembers it well.

He was mindful of midfielder Cavan Sullivan's mood earlier this season. Sullivan was finding playing time hard to come by for a side that was struggling mightily. Even as Richter was spending most of his time managing the Union's reserve team, he couldn't help but notice the demeanor of a player he first coached as an 8-year-old.

"He was pissed," Richter said of Sullivan in an interview with ESPN. "He wanted a chance to play."

He eventually got it, and he has been taking out that anger on the rest of MLS ever since.

As Sullivan and the Union head into this weekend's game against FC Cincinnati, the 17-year-old is nursing an ankle injury, but his rise has been the story of the MLS season. His 21 goal contributions have already broken the league record for a teenager, eclipsing the 20 recorded by the New England Revolution's Diego Fagundez in 2013. Ditto for goal contributions by a player younger than 17, with Sullivan -- who turned 17 in late September -- breaking the mark of 10 set by Freddy Adu in 2005.

His success has been accompanied by a feistiness, his brilliance often combined with a snarl. Such success has led to chatter that since the resumption of league play following the FIFA World Cup, Sullivan is the league MVP, non-Lionel Messi division.

There is a case to be made for slotting him in just behind the former Argentina captain given the Union's change in fortunes. Prior to the World Cup break, Philadelphia was dead last in MLS, with just seven points from 15 matches. Since the break, the Union have a league-best 39 points thanks to a 12-3-1 record and clinched a playoff spot on Wednesday. That the run has coincided with Sullivan's ascension is by no means a fluke.

When the subject of Sullivan's MVP candidacy is brought up to Richter, one can almost hear the grimace over the phone. Part of Richter's job description these days is to slow the collective roll surrounding his young star, and he's not about to stop now.

"There's time to look back and reflect on stuff like that after the season," Richter said about the MVP talk. "Forget about all the other outside noise of what could be. Let's have a f---ing great session today."

Numbers have also served to cool the MVP talk. According to TruMedia -- which doesn't count secondary assists to the same degree that MLS does -- Sullivan's 15 goal contributions since the World Cup break has him seventh in the league, behind such luminaries as Orlando City SC's Antoine Griezmann (22) and Messi (19). Sullivan's contributions aren't even the most on his own team, with Milan Iloski (18) leading the way. Other players, such as Cincinnati's Evander and Hany Mukhtar of the Supporters' Shield-winning Nashville SC have been utterly consistent over the course of the campaign.

The MVP moniker also gets thrown around rather casually, and with Messi taking up so much of the league's oxygen, it's an easy label to affix to a player like Sullivan who is enjoying a stellar run of form. In some respects, the chatter doesn't do Sullivan any favors. He's still just a teenager -- albeit an extraordinarily talented one -- and the MVP label doesn't tell the whole story of his season.

Sullivan's production seemingly came out of nowhere. His 14 league appearances prior to this season yielded no goal contributions. He had just five in MLS play in 13 league appearances through the end of May, but he logged just 549 minutes. There certainly wasn't any MVP talk during the first half of 2026.

Yet Sullivan's rise wasn't something that just happened. It was the result of some meticulous planning on the part of the Union from the time they signed Sullivan as a 14-year-old, as well as the player's hard work. Every step, from the academy and through the reserve team to the first team, was carefully choreographed. While it's easy to draw a demarcation line pre- and post-World Cup, there were signs of a breakthrough prior to the pause for the tournament, as Sullivan began to get on the field with more consistency. That extended playing time freed up his mind to begin playing closer to his best.

"In the very beginning of the season, if [Sullivan] got 10 minutes here and there, he would try to fit everything into those 10 minutes, and it's hard to play like that," Richter said. "And then towards the end -- I would say the end of the first half of the season -- when he got some extended runs and a couple starts, then he really showed that he could do something at this level."

When Richter took over after manager Bradley Carnell was fired at the end of May, he decided there was no way he was taking Sullivan out of the lineup.

"The first conversation with [Sullivan] was just that he's going to get the chance now, like a real chance, not just put him in and see how he does," Richter said. "It's, 'Cav, I believe that you are a great player at this level and I believe that you can be. Now you get a real opportunity with coaches who believe that fully, and you've got to take it.'"

Sullivan didn't wait for the regular season to try to repay that faith. His mentality has long been one of his best traits, and he was determined to maximize the time that the World Cup break afforded him. He played a match for Union II against the Ivory Coast prior to the World Cup, a period when most of the roster was on vacation. He trained with his brother, Quinn Sullivan, and his father Brendan, a former pro player, to maintain his fitness. He then played in four friendlies against MLS opposition, and impressed every time.

"That was an important period for [Sullivan] because he gained the respect of everybody," Richter said. "And then when the season started, it was no question of 'does he deserve to start?' Of course he deserves to start. He can be a difference maker for us at this level."

Even then, Sullivan's emergence was a bit of a slow burn. He had no goal contributions in his first four matches post-break, but a goal and assist against Necaxa in the Leagues Cup got him going, and there have been no shortage of highlight-reel moments since, for both club and country. These included an audacious back-heel for a goal against San Diego FC that showed jaw-dropping levels of skill and improvisation. Those traits were on display for the United States team against Mexico, when he stole an errant pass from El Tri keeper Raúl Rangel and lobbed him from 35 yards.

Even if Sullivan's campaign has been a few notches below MVP caliber, it has still been a season to savor, and a new face excelling in the league is always compelling. There's also the fact that MLS and the Union won't have Sullivan for much longer; he's slated to join Manchester City in January 2028, shortly after his 18th birthday. With the league calendar changing, all that's left of Sullivan's time in MLS is the 2027 sprint season and the first half of the 2027-28 campaign.

The impulse, then, is to enjoy Sullivan's presence in the league -- and shower him with praise -- for as long as it lasts. And who knows what the next 15 months will bring? This year's MLS Young Player of the Year award seems well within reach, but any future success is predicated on making the most of the present. With the postseason approaching, that is the challenge facing Sullivan and the Union coaching staff.

"This game changes so quick. If you look where the last five months have taken him, where's five months from now?" Richter said about Sullivan. "We have to continue to push every single day, focus on getting better.

"A lot can change in a few months, so let's make that a positive change. Every week that goes by, let's make it a positive. Let's make another step forward. That's my responsibility as his coach, is to continue to help him taking steps forward. I know he has a mentality that he'll continue to push to do that."

If Sullivan does that, then trophies of all sorts should come his way.

stories.headline: Lens fans banned from Liverpool match for throwing flares vs. Brugge
stories.summary: Fans of Ligue 1 club Lens were banned from buying tickets for a Champions League game at Liverpool by a UEFA disciplinary ruling Tuesday.
stories.body:
NYON, Switzerland -- Fans of Ligue 1 club Lens were banned from buying tickets for a Champions League game at Liverpool by a UEFA disciplinary ruling on Tuesday.

Lens fans lit dozens of flares and threw some toward rival supporters and the field, forcing the team's Champions League game at Club Brugge last week to be stopped briefly. Lens lost 3-0.

The club already were on probation by UEFA for fans lighting flares and fireworks at a previous Champions League game at Slavia Prague in September.

UEFA said its appeals judges imposed a ban on Lens selling tickets to fans for two Champions League away games.

The sanction will be served when Lens play at Leipzig on Nov. 24 and at Liverpool at Anfield on Jan. 27. A third game ban is deferred for a two-year probationary period.

UEFA said Lens were fined €80,000 ($89,000) for charges of "lighting and throwing of pyrotechnics as well as for acts of damage."

stories.headline: Power to burn and a 'trademark' goal: why Ethan Drever has rocketed up draft boards
stories.summary: Growing up an Essendon supporter, Ethan Drever hasn't 'seen anything' like success. But his rise up draft boards could have him in the frame to be his childhood club's first pick, writes Jasper Chellappah.
stories.body:
Ethan Drever had absolutely no choice on his AFL team. As a newborn he was put in an Essendon jumper at the hospital and he's been a Bomber ever since.

It's been a rough 18 years of fandom since, and he's got some thoughts about his dad's decision.

"I'm [born in] 2008, I haven't seen anything!" he tells ESPN with a grin - and a grimace.

"Dad tells me about his success and I'm like, 'You don't have to rub it in like that.'"

The Dons are entering a new era in 2027 under Mark McVeigh and it's being driven through the draft. They snagged Sullivan Robey, Jacob Farrow, and Dyson Sharp in the first round 12 months ago and now own pick 1 in the upcoming draft.

Drever also has a lot of thoughts about those drafted before him.

"They've got some good young boys in there now. Robey, Sharp, they're gonna be so good.

"I like Farrow. He should be kicking in and doing all that, he needs to be in priority positions. That's what he's gonna be doing in the future.

"Just that halfback, I reckon he's gonna be really good... he's a beautiful left foot kick."

After a dour two-win season the Bombers have first call on Drever, with the 188cm on-baller strongly linked at the top of the board.

He's an electric runner with the intent to tackle, chase, and pressure - something that hasn't been a trait of Essendon's list for a long time.

Asked what he thinks when watching his boyhood club each weekend, Drever's response would prick the ears of all Bombers fans.

"It'd be nice to be out there and sort of help the boys out, that's kinda what I'm thinking!"

The Vic Country MVP and Rebels best and fairest produced a remarkable season. His star has risen from a first-round chance to the very top of the open pool.

He may have the most translatable traits to AFL level of any prospect. Drever is an elite power athlete, recording a 2.92 second 20 metre sprint which comes across in the tape. He bursts out of the contest with driving legs and loves to exit forward of the stoppage to inflict maximum damage.

His ultra consistent season has come about without any injury concerns, something all other top prospects this year haven't been able to say.

"It's been good not to have to sit on the sidelines this year at all and I can just keep playing consistent footy," he says.

"I only missed one [game] which was just after champs, I just had a break."

Drever lays claim to a pretty handy trademark. On six separate occasions this season he's collected the ball -- either out of a stoppage or in open play -- and powered away from opponents into the forward half of the ground.

From there his long running gait and elite top speed helps him separate from chasing defenders and break the paint of 50 to drive home sensational goals.

"I have heard it's called the trademark goal now. I don't know where that's really come from, it's just a natural thing I guess. I just like to run and have a ping from outside 50," Drever tells ESPN.

"Definitely one of my traits is just my power, especially this year. Building up over the pre-season and definitely my two-way running.

"It's the long-term goal to move into the midfield and be a bit of a Jordan Dawson with his two-way running. I love Finn Callaghan, how he plays. Those two are really great role models for me.

"I think Hugh McCluggage as well, I've watched him a lot. I had a meeting with him this year, he's that sort of two-way runner as well and he's been really good for me."

Drever played 13 games for the Rebels this year in amongst commitments with the AFL Academy and Vic Country. He collected the ball 28 times to go with a goal a game, but he's not satisfied with just being an offensive weapon.

The Ballarat local is a tenacious presence in contests with the appetite to chase and tackle, racking up 6.5 per outing to frank his status as the best pure midfielder in the open pool.

At the draft combine he showed off a much-improved engine running a 6:27 minute 2km after going 20 seconds slower in the lead-up. It's a time that will put him towards the front of the pack on day one of pre-season.

Drever knows exactly what's required to be a midfielder at the next level, and he's determined to get there as soon as possible.

"My endurance side was a big goal of mine, obviously at the top level you've just got to be able to run all day.

"Honing in on my fundamentals and trying to get them the best I can as well. That's what the most important thing is because it's the little one percenters that make a difference in the AFL.

Drever is now on the precipice of living out his dream of becoming an AFL player, and it could be for his boyhood club as the top choice in the open pool of the draft.

That won't matter to him, so long as he gets his opportunity to shine on the big stage.

"I don't really care [if I go at pick 1]. It's nice to have my name up in consideration alongside those boys but I'll just be happy to be picked up wherever I go."

stories.headline: Salkilld, Saint Denis to headline UFC Fight Night in Sydney
stories.summary: West Australian Quillan Salkilld will headline a UFC Fight Night lightweight matchup with Benoît Saint Denis in Sydney in February.
stories.body:
West Australian Quillan Salkilld will return to the Octagon in Sydney, after it was confirmed he'll headline the UFC Fight Night with a lightweight bout against Frenchman Benoît Saint Denis on February 7 (AEDT).

Salkilld, 26, is a former Australian rules footballer who turned to MMA after leaving school at 16, and boasts an impressive 13-1 professional record (6-0 in UFC) with five 'performance of the night' bonuses.

The Broome native has won four consecutive fights with a first-round finish, most recently submitting Mateusz Gamrot in their UFC Fight Night clash in Perth in August. He's widely regarded as Australia's next big combat star.

Meanwhile Saint Denis, 30, is one of the lightweight division's most dangerous finishers, and has a 17-4 professional record.

Peter Kloczko, senior vice president of UFC Australia and New Zealand, said the Fight Night -- to take place at Sydney's Afterpay Arena -- would be an "unforgettable event" featuring one of Australia's brightest young stars.

"UFC Fight Night Sydney is set to be another huge moment for Australian fans, and Quillan Salkilld versus Benoît Saint Denis is a main event that delivers everything we look for in this sport," he said in the official release.

"Quillan has been one of the breakout stars of the UFC's lightweight division, while Benoît is one of the most dangerous and exciting finishers in the sport. Bringing this fight to Sydney will make for an unforgettable night."

Further fights on the card will be released in due course.

stories.headline: Daly Cherry-Evans won't consider NRL backflip, backs Roosters' Sam Walker move
stories.summary: Without making any promises, Daly Cherry-Evans has ruled out a second season at the Sydney Roosters, while backing the NRL premiers' hardline stance against Sam Walker.
stories.body:
Without making any promises, Daly Cherry-Evans has ruled out a second season at the Sydney Roosters, while backing the NRL premiers' hardline stance against Sam Walker.

Bound for the English Super League, Cherry-Evans insists he has not fielded any phone calls from Roosters coach Trent Robinson or chairman Nick Politis in the wake of the club pulling its multi-million-dollar deal to Walker to remain beyond 2027.

But even if he does, the 37-year-old won't be answering any potential SOS call from the Tricolours.

"No, it's all done. It's all done," Cherry-Evans said on Thursday.

"Look, I'm so proud of my time at the Roosters, but you won't be seeing me back there as a player."

Asked if he promised, the veteran playmaker said "No", but maintained he was content with ending his 16-season NRL career as it started, with a second premiership to go with his 2011 triumph with Manly.

Speaking from experience, having reneged on a lucrative 10-year deal to join Gold Coast to remain at Manly early in his career, Cherry-Evans said he didn't find Walker's situation sad at all.

"Maybe I'm a little too emotionless with these things," he said.

"It's the game, it's the business. I really admire the way that the Roosters have stood their ground on what they believe to be right for the club.

"That's one thing that has really shone through at my time here, is that they will put the club first over any one individual.

"And then from my point of view on Sam, Sam's doing what's best for him and his family and his future, so that's the thing within all of this is - no one's actually done anything wrong.

"Yeah, the emotions get really high and we all want to see people stay and we don't want to see people leave, and I get it, but at the end of the day, no one's doing anything wrong here.

"This is just a contract negotiation."

Cherry-Evans said, as good mates, he'd been in contact this week with Walker, who is in World Cup camp with the Kangaroos in Townsville, and revealed that his grand final-winning halves partner is remaining positive.

"It's hard to rattle Sammy, or maybe he'll never let you know how much he is stressed, or not doing OK," Cherry-Evans said.

"But from what I understand in my conversations with him, he's going well. He's got good family and friends around him.

"I would back Sam to have a really long career in the NRL. We all wanted to see it happen at the Roosters and I'm sure there's a chance it could happen and still happen, but it's a game, it's a business.

"I know we'd love to see our players play for one club, but the likelihood and the reality of that, it just doesn't happen often anymore."

If the Roosters do release Walker from the remaining year of his contract as the Queensland and new Australia representative becomes a free agent on Sunday, youngster Toby Rodwell is being earmarked as the likely No.7 replacement.

"I love Toby Rodwell, and I think he's got a great future ahead," Cherry-Evans said.

"But I'm not playing hypotheticals with you."
